title: Local Gaussian Correlation in the Tails: A Scarcity Diagnostic, an Optimal Local Bandwidth, and the Limits of Adaptivity

p.t: Dependence between financial assets is not constant across their range: equities that are nearly uncorrelated in calm markets crash together in a crisis. Capturing this requires a local measure of dependence. Local Gaussian correlation (Tjøstheim and Hufthammer, 2013;Berentsen et al., 2014b) provides one: at each point of the sample space it fits a bivariate Gaussian by kernelweighted local likelihood and reads off the correlation ρ(x), yielding a full dependence surface that reduces to the global correlation only when the data are jointly Gaussian. LGC has been used to re-examine financial contagion (Støve et al., 2014), allocate portfolios under asymmetric dependence (Sleire et al., 2022), and detect regime changes (Gundersen et al., 2024). The difficulty is that LGC is least reliable where it is most valuable. A local estimator needs observations in the local neighbourhood, and the joint tails are by definition sparse. The natural lever is the bandwidth, and one might hope a location-adaptive bandwidth that widens in the tails would help. It largely does not: an adaptive bandwidth was tried for the locally Gaussian density estimator and found inferior to a single global selector (Otneim and Tjøstheim, 2017), and global bandwidths remain the default. This paper explains that experience and bounds it. We identify what governs tail error, derive the AMISE-optimal local bandwidth for LGC, and map the narrow regime in which location-adaptivity helps and the wider regimes in which it does not.

Our contributions: 1. The marginal transform is inert ( §3). Fitting a heavy-tailed parametric marginal before LGC, a natural-seeming fix for fat-tailed data, changes the integrated error only in the fourth decimal. The lever is not the marginal. 2. A scarcity diagnostic ( §4). Tail scarcity has been noted informally (Jordanger and Tjøstheim, 2022); we make it precise. LGC error is organised by the local effective sample size eff_n(x), not by the estimator variant, and its dispersion obeys a Fisher variance floor sd ≈ (1 -ρ 2 )/ √ eff_n. This identifies the bandwidth as the operative lever. 3. An AMISE-optimal local bandwidth ( §5). We derive b ⋆ (x) ∝ [(1-ρ 2 ) 2 /(f β 2 )] 1/6 n -1/6 by balancing the local-likelihood bias against this variance floor. To our knowledge this is the first AMISE-optimal, location-specific bandwidth derived for the LGC estimator; we validate its bias expansion directly. Prior LGC bandwidths are global, and the one prior adaptive attempt was an ad hoc nearest-neighbour device found inferior to the global selector (Otneim and Tjøstheim, 2017).

A Monte Carlo across dependence strengths shows the adaptive rule beats the global plug-in only at moderate dependence with curved surfaces. At weak dependence the surface is flat and redistribution only adds variance; at strong dependence the surface is steep and finite-sample bias dominates, making adaptivity substantially worse with an error that grows in the sample size; an oracle-scale experiment shows this failure is intrinsic to the pointwise-optimal shape, not to our normalisation. This explains why global bandwidths have been hard to beat, and locates the exception. On real equity returns ( §8) the adaptive estimator is more stable under resampling, a use that does not require beating global on accuracy. The common thread: tail LGC is bounded by data scarcity, which a bandwidth can redistribute but not overcome.

p.s: Background: the LGC estimator and its bandwidth
p.t: LGC fits, at a point x, a bivariate Gaussian ψ(• ; θ) with θ = (µ 1 , µ 2 , σ 1 , σ 2 , ρ) by maximising the kernel-weighted local log-likelihood of Hjort and Jones (1996), with a product kernel The maximiser θ(x) defines the local Gaussian correlation ρ(x). In practice each margin is first mapped to standard normality by the empirical normal-score transform, so the estimator operates on Gaussian pseudo-observations (Berentsen et al., 2014b); §3 shows this choice of marginal transform is immaterial.

Bandwidth selection for LGC has, to date, been global. Two choices dominate: a global likelihood cross-validation (Berentsen and Tjøstheim, 2014;Otneim and Tjøstheim, 2017) and a fast plug-in b 0 = 1.75 n -1/6 whose rate follows from the local-likelihood asymptotics and whose constant is fixed empirically (Tjøstheim and Hufthammer, 2013); both are the only options in the standard software (Berentsen et al., 2014a) and underpin the methodology of the reference monograph (Tjøstheim et al., 2022). A point-dependent k-nearest-neighbour bandwidth was tried in the locally Gaussian density setting but found inferior to the global selector and not pursued (Otneim and Tjøstheim, 2017), and the data-scarcity of distributional tails has been noted only informally, with "use a larger bandwidth" offered as the remedy (Jordanger and Tjøstheim, 2022). To our knowledge, no prior work derives a bias-variance-balanced, location-specific bandwidth for the LGC estimator itself; that is the gap this paper fills. We write the local effective sample size eff_n(x) the number of observations that contribute meaningfully to the local fit; it is the quantity the rest of the paper turns on.

Unless stated otherwise, simulations use four copulas (Gaussian, Clayton, t 4 , Gumbel) parameterised to Kendall's τ = 0.5, pushed through symmetric unitvariance normal tempered stable marginals (Rachev et al., 2011), with R = 50 replications at n ∈ {500, 1000, 2500, 5000} (the dependence sweep of §7.2 varies τ and uses R = 25). "Ground truth" is LGC on an auxiliary n gt = 20,000 sample, evaluated on an 11 × 11 grid over [-3, 3] 2 plus five diagonal quantile points z q = (Φ -1 (q), Φ -1 (q)), q ∈ {.01, .05, .5, .95, .99}. Accuracy is the density-weighted integrated squared error (ISE) over the grid; tail behaviour is read at the quantile points.

Heavy-tailed marginal models are standard in financial econometrics (Barndorff-Nielsen, 1997;Cont and Tankov, 2004;Rachev et al., 2011;Deep et al., 2025), so a natural hypothesis is that fitting a parametric heavy-tailed marginal before estimating LGC, rather than using the empirical transform, should sharpen the tail estimates. We test this with three estimators differing only in the marginal step: canonical (empirical CDF), an oracle that transforms through the true marginal CDF, and a version that fits the marginal by maximum likelihood. Because the oracle carries no marginal-estimation error by construction, the canonical-oracle gap isolates the transform's contribution. That gap is negligible. At n = 5000 the three estimators agree to the fourth decimal of density-weighted ISE in every copula (Table 1, Figure 1), while the tail sampling error is one to two orders of magnitude larger. This quantifies, under heavy tempered-stable tails, the marginal-invariance already implicit in the standard practice of estimating LGC on normalscore pseudo-observations (Berentsen et al., 2014b): local dependence is a copula property, so the marginal transform contributes only estimation noise. Nor does asymmetry change this: repeating the comparison with a skewed NTS marginal (β = -0.6, skewness ≈ -0.84; n = 2500, R = 25) leaves the three estimators within 0.0003-0.0014 of one another in ISE across all four copulas; the conclusion is unchanged. The marginal is not the lever; we fix the canonical empirical transform hereafter and ask what is.

p.s: The binding constraint is local scarcity
p.t: If neither the estimator variant nor the marginal separates the cells, what governs the error? The local effective sample size (2). That distributional tails are data-poor for LGC has been remarked before, informally, with a larger bandwidth suggested as the countermeasure (Jordanger and Tjøstheim, 2022); here we make the observation quantitative. Two facts stand out (Figure 2). First, error is organised by eff_n, not by the estimator: within each cell the RMSE spread across the three estimators of §3 has median 0.005, while eff_n itself falls from ∼ 160-1000 at the centre to as few as ∼ 7 in the tails. Second, the dispersion is a Fisher variance floor. The replication standard deviation follows sd ≈ (1 -ρ 2 )/ √ eff_n; regressing log[sd/(1 -ρ 2 )] on log eff_n gives slope -0.61 with R 2 = 0.76. This matches the asymptotic variance of a Gaussian-correlation maximum likelihood estimator from m observations, Var(ρ) ≈ (1 -ρ 2 ) 2 /m, with m = eff_n the local count. The fitted slope is somewhat steeper than the theoretical -1/2; the excess is consistent with the sparsest cells, where the floor is least clean and bias contaminates the dispersion, pulling the pooled slope down. Most tail error is therefore variance, and variance is bought back by raising eff_n. Bias dominates only at the sharply-structured sparse corners; the clearest is Clayton at q = 0.99 (true local ρ ≈ -0.68, eff_n ≈ 7), where RMSE ≈ 0.76 but |bias| ≈ 0.60 ≳ sd ≈ 0.48. This is the regime no bandwidth can rescue, and we return to it below.

p.s: The binding constraint is local scarcity
p.t: The consequence for design: a bandwidth that raises eff_n in the tails has real headroom against the variance floor, but widening blindly trades variance for bias wherever the surface is not locally constant. The LGC estimator is an instance of the Hjort and Jones (1996) local-likelihood estimator, so its bias and variance follow from that theory specialized to the five-parameter Gaussian family. The two ingredients exist separately in the LGC literature: the leading O(b 2 ) bias of the local Gaussian likelihood estimator was derived by Otneim et al. (2013), and the asymptotic covariance of the local-correlation maximum likelihood estimator was given by Otneim and Tjøstheim (2022). Our contribution here is to assemble them into the first explicit local-AMISE balance for ρ(x). Under standard conditions (f smooth and bounded away from 0 near x; b → 0, nb 2 → ∞), the correlation component satisfies with kernel constants µ 2 (K) = u 2 K, R(K) = K 2 . The variance factor (1 -ρ 2 ) 2 is the per-observation asymptotic variance of the Gaussian-correlation MLE; dividing by the local count (2) reproduces the empirical Fisher floor of §4, tying the diagnostic to the theory. The bias functional, to leading order, combines the Laplacian of the local-correlation surface (the curvature term) with a random-design density-drift term and a model-misfit remainder r that vanishes where f is locally Gaussian. §5.4 validates (4) directly; the exact closed-form constant in (5), a full specialization of Hjort-Jones to the Gaussian family, is deferred to future work and is not needed for the bandwidth, which is invariant to it ( §6).

The local asymptotic mean squared error is, from ( 3)-(4), Minimising over b yields the location-specific optimum. Theorem 1 (AMISE-optimal LGC bandwidth). The bandwidth minimising the local AMSE ( 6) The optimal rate n -1/6 matches the canonical global plug-in; what is new is the locationspecific constant. The bandwidth widens in sparse regions (∝ f -1/6 ), narrows where the surface is structured (∝ β -1/3 , the curvature penalty), and narrows toward the dependence extremes (∝ (1 -ρ 2 ) 1/3 ): where |ρ| → 1 the per-observation variance (1 -ρ 2 ) 2 collapses, so less local averaging is needed. §7 shows the cost of this last property: the over-narrowing, and the compensating over-widening it forces elsewhere, is what makes the rule misbehave when the whole surface is strongly dependent.

A natural way to make the LGC bandwidth adaptive is to import the Brockmann et al. (1993) curvature/variance balance from one-dimensional kernel regression, part of a long variablebandwidth tradition in density and regression smoothing (Breiman et al., 1977;Abramson, 1982;Loader, 1996), augmented with the random-design density widening of Fan and Gijbels (1996); doing so gives b heur ∝ (1 -ρ 2 ) 1/6 f -1/6 κ -1/3 with κ = ∥∇ 2 ρ∥. Theorem 1 shows two corrections are required. The dependence factor is (1 -ρ 2 ) 1/3 , not (1 -ρ 2 ) 1/6 : the borrowed rule takes a square root too few, because the LGC variance scales as (1 -ρ 2 ) 2 rather than (1 -ρ 2 ). And the curvature is the signed functional β of ( 5), with its density-drift term, rather than the Frobenius Hessian norm κ. The first correction makes the rule narrow more aggressively at high |ρ|. As §7 shows, this helps at moderate dependence, where the corrected rule improves on the heuristic, and hurts at strong dependence, where the same aggressiveness destabilises it.

p.s: Numerical validation of the bias expansion
p.t: Equation ( 4) is the load-bearing assumption behind Theorem 1, so we test it directly. For curved-surface copulas (Clayton, Gumbel) we sweep a ladder of bandwidths, averaging ρ(x; b) over 120 replications at each b (n = 4000), and at each grid point regress the mean estimate on b 2 ; its slope estimates 1 2 µ 2 β(x) without reference to the unknown ρ 0 (the intercept). Both halves hold (Figure 3). The rate: the per-point fits are strongly linear in b 2 (median R 2 = 0.93 and 0.90 for the two copulas). The structure: the empirical bias slope is proportional to the predicted β(x) of (5), correlation 0.80 over 73 points, sign-correct through the origin. The fitted proportionality constant (0.34) sits below the nominal µ 2 /2, as expected: the exact Hjort-Jones constant carries projection factors beyond µ 2 /2, and estimating β by finite differences on a pilot grid attenuates any such regression slope toward zero. The form underlying (7), which is all the bandwidth requires, is confirmed. ) is proportional to the predicted β(x) (correlation 0.80, through-origin fit shown), confirming the bias structure.

Theorem 1 is operationalised by plug-in. All three location functionals come from a single global-bandwidth pilot fit: the density f from the pilot eff_n via (2); 1 -ρ2 from the pilot surface; and β = ∆ρ+2 ∇ log f ⊤ ∇ρ by finite differences. Two design choices keep the comparison fair and the procedure stable.

We normalise the per-point constant so that its density-weighted geometric mean equals the global plug-in constant. The adaptive rule then redistributes a fixed smoothing budget (wider tails, narrower centre) rather than globally inflating it, so any gain is attributable to placement, not to more smoothing. This also makes b ⋆ invariant to the unknown overall constant C K and to the closed-form constant in β. Curvature stabilisation. Because β sits in a denominator, a near-empty, sharply-structured tail could otherwise produce a runaway window. We smooth β at a coarse scale, floor it away from zero, and cap the per-point bandwidth to [0.5, 3]× the global value; these are the stabilisers Brockmann et al. (1993) show are necessary for an estimated local bandwidth.

p.s: When does adaptivity help? A Monte Carlo
p.t: We compare the global plug-in against the adaptive rules on shared samples (a paired design that removes sampling noise from the differences). Two questions: at the conventional moderate dependence, whether and where adaptivity helps ( §7.1); and across dependence strength, the regime in which it helps at all ( §7.2).

At Kendall's τ = 0.5 the adaptive rules improve the density-weighted ISE on the copulas whose surface has curvature to exploit (Clayton, t 4 , Gumbel), the gain growing with n to 13-14% at n = 5000, while costing 2-14% on the near-flat Gaussian surface, where redistribution can only add variance (Figure 4a). A second effect was not designed for: the adaptive estimator has the smaller replication standard deviation in 11 of the 16 (copula, n) cells, and in every cell with n ≥ 2500. Once the pilot fields are well estimated, it stabilises the surface across samples. Against local eff_n, the picture is the one §4 predicts: adaptive is taxed below a few dozen effective observations (an estimated local bandwidth costs O p (n -1/2 ) variability against O p (n -1 ) for a global one) and reaches parity-or-better above. Corrected rule versus the heuristic. Still at τ = 0.5, the derived rule also improves on the borrowed heuristic, and where the theory predicts: the corrected (1 -ρ 2 ) 1/3 exponent helps most in the strongly-dependent, sparse tail (Table 2, Figure 4b). Pooling the quantile-point cells by local eff_n, the corrected rule improves on the heuristic by a median 10% in the band eff_n ∈ [15, 40) (93% of cells) and 6.5% in [40, 120) (81% of cells), while matching it in the dense bulk (eff_n ≥ 120) and at the hopeless deepest tail (eff_n < 15). Restricted to strongly-dependent sparse cells (|ρ| ≥ 0.5, eff_n ≤ 40), the corrected rule beats the heuristic on 77% of cells, median -5.7%. The effect is modest but predicted and consistent. At the single worst cell (Clayton q = 0.99, eff_n ≈ 7) all three estimators are tied; this is the bias-dominated regime no bandwidth can cure.

p.s: Across dependence strength: the regime of applicability
p.t: The moderate-dependence picture does not generalise. We sweep Kendall's τ ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 0.8}, comparing the global plug-in with the derived AMISE rule on shared samples (25 replications per cell at τ ∈ {0.2, 0.8}; the τ = 0.5 column reuses the run above). The adaptive advantage is confined to a band (Figure 5): • Weak dependence (τ = 0.2): adaptive is worse than global or at best at parity (+6 to +13% ISE at n = 5000 for Gaussian, Clayton and Gumbel; -0.7% for t 4 ; +14 to +18% for all four copulas at n = 500). The surface is nearly flat, so there is little curvature to exploit and redistribution mostly adds variance: the Gaussian story of §7.1, now for essentially all copulas. • Moderate dependence (τ = 0.5): adaptive wins on the curved copulas, the only regime in which it does. • Strong dependence (τ = 0.8): on the curved copulas adaptive is markedly worse (+95% for Clayton, +139% for t 4 , +70% for Gumbel at n = 5000; the near-flat Gaussian is the lone exception at -6%), and the gap grows with n (Figure 5b), the signature of bias rather than variance. The mechanism of the strong-dependence failure. The causal chain has three links. First, on a strongly dependent surface the optimal rule (7) narrows sharply along the dense, high-|ρ| ridge: the per-observation variance (1 -ρ 2 ) 2 is small there, so the pointwise bias-variance trade favours little smoothing. Second, the narrowing collides with the smoothing budget: because the normalisation pins the (density-weighted geometric) mean bandwidth, the budget freed on the ridge must be spent elsewhere, and it lands on the steep mid-region, driving bandwidths into the upper cap (36% of grid points at τ = 0.8, versus none in the dense bulk at τ = 0.5). Third, the over-widened windows average across genuinely varying correlation, producing bias, and bias does not shrink as n grows; hence the deficit in Figure 5b widens with the sample size. Three checks localise the fault. A region-by-region decomposition puts the loss in the dense centre and mid-range (each ≈ 2.9× the global ISE), not the sparse corners. Tripling the pilot-grid resolution for β barely moves it (2.4× → 2.2× global), ruling out curvature estimation as the cause. And the failure is intrinsic to the shape of ( 7), not to the budget-neutral normalisation: keeping the AMISE shape, discarding budget neutrality entirely, and sweeping a global multiplier over the shape (an oracle scale, which upper-bounds any data-driven normalisation), the best multiplier still loses to the global plug-in by +42% (Clayton) and +51% (t 4 ) at τ = 0.8, n = 2500 on paired samples. Freeing the scale narrows the budget-neutral deficit (for t 4 , ISE 0.149 → 0.128 against global 0.085) but closes nowhere near the gap: on a steep, strongly dependent surface the pointwise-optimal allocation itself missmooths, and no choice of overall scale repairs it. This is the mechanism behind the field's experience that the global bandwidth is hard to beat for LGC (Otneim and Tjøstheim, 2017): outside a moderate-dependence, curved-surface band a single global bandwidth is preferable, and the strong-dependence deficit is large. The scarcity diagnostic of §4 explains why: tail error is variance-floored, and only where a curved surface permits trading bias for variance at adequate eff_n can a location-varying bandwidth improve the trade. At τ = 0.8 the deficit grows with n for the curved copulas (a bias signature), while the Gaussian is again the exception.

The Monte Carlo isolates the adaptive bandwidth's behaviour against a known truth. On real data no such truth exists, so we are deliberate about what can be claimed. Two things can be shown without a ground-truth surface: that the global and adaptive estimators resolve the tail dependence differently, in a way consistent with the simulation; and, quantitatively, that the adaptive surface is more stable under resampling. The second is the real-data analogue of the Monte Carlo finding that at moderate-to-large samples the adaptive estimator carries the smaller replication standard deviation ( §7.1), and it is the headline here because it needs no truth. We do not claim a real-data accuracy gain, which would not be identifiable.

We take daily adjusted closes for two pairs with distinct dependence geometry: SPY versus long-dated Treasuries (TLT), the sign-varying flight-to-quality relationship; and SPY versus emerging-market equity (EEM), strong positive dependence with lower-tail crisis contagion, the canonical setting of the local Gaussian contagion literature (Støve et al., 2014). The sample runs 2005-2024 (n = 5030 common trading days after filtering), spanning the 2008 and 2020 crises so the joint tails are populated.

LGC on raw returns would partly measure common volatility rather than dependence. Following the contagion literature we pre-whiten each series with an AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) model with Student-t innovations and estimate LGC on the standardised residuals (Table 3). The Ljung-Box statistics confirm the filter removes both serial correlation and volatility clustering, while the residuals retain the heavy tails and asymmetry that carry the dependence of interest. The marginal step is then the canonical empirical normal-score transform; Result 1 (the parametric transform is inert) is what licenses this simpler choice over a refitted NTS margin. Figure 6 shows the LGC surfaces, global versus adaptive, with the sparse tails (local effective sample size below the Monte Carlo floor of 15) masked so the comparison is read only where either estimator has support. The qualitative reading matches the simulation. For SPY/TLT the bulk dependence is negative, with the local correlation strengthening and changing character toward the corners; the adaptive estimator, spending its fixed smoothing budget outward, presents the off-centre structure more coherently while the global surface is granular there. For SPY/EEM the dependence is strongly positive throughout, and the difference panel is almost one-signed in the tails: the adaptive estimator resolves stronger joint-tail correlation than the global one, which over-smooths and speckles in the same sparse region. This is the expected effect, redistribution toward the tails, on data where, unlike the simulation, we cannot grade it against a truth.

Because the GARCH step pre-whitens to near-i.i.d. residuals, we resample the residual pairs i.i.d. with replacement (B = 200) and recompute both surfaces on each resample. Figure 7 plots the point-wise bootstrap standard deviation ratio, adaptive over global, against local effective sample size. The ratio sits below one across most of the grid and falls furthest in the sparse tail, the regime the adaptive rule targets: median ratio 0.93 for SPY/TLT and 0.74 for SPY/EEM, dropping to 0.83 and 0.52 respectively in the tail band (eff_n < 40); the adaptive surface is more stable on 61% and 72% of the supported grid. The deep, near-empty corners are excluded (both estimators are undefined there), so this is not a boundary artefact. The simulation's stabilisation result thus carries over to real returns, and it does so most where it matters, in the data-starved tails. p.s: What the application does and does not establish
p.t: On real data the adaptive bandwidth produces tail-dependence surfaces that are quantitatively more stable under resampling, the gain concentrated in the sparse tails. What it cannot establish, here or anywhere without a known truth, is a tail-accuracy improvement. This caveat is sharper given the regime map of §7.2: the SPY/EEM pair is strongly dependent, the very regime in which adaptivity trades variance for bias, so its lower resampling dispersion may partly reflect over-smoothing rather than better accuracy. We therefore claim only the variance property (more stable surfaces) and not improved estimation. The deepest corners, finally, remain beyond reach for either estimator, the same eff_n floor seen in the Monte Carlo: the binding constraint is genuine scarcity, which no bandwidth cures.

Our findings form one arc. The binding constraint on tail LGC is local scarcity, not the marginal model; scarcity expresses itself as a Fisher variance floor; that floor is the variance term of the local AMISE; and minimising the AMISE yields a location-specific optimal bandwidth. But the same derivation explains why that bandwidth is not a panacea: a location-varying bandwidth can only redistribute local sample size, and that helps the bias-variance trade only where the surface is curved enough to make the trade worthwhile and populated enough to make it stable. That band, moderate dependence, is narrow, and outside it a single global bandwidth is preferable, sharply so at strong dependence. Our study turns the field's informal experience (an adaptive bandwidth was tried and found inferior; global selection is the default) into a quantitative account of why and where. The contribution is therefore threefold: a diagnostic that identifies the variance floor, the first AMISE-optimal local bandwidth for LGC together with its validated bias expansion, and a map of the one regime in which location-adaptivity pays. The boundaries are as informative as the band. On a flat surface (weak dependence) redistribution only adds variance; on a steep surface (strong dependence) it incurs bias that grows with the sample size; and in the deepest, near-empty corners no bandwidth manufactures information the data do not contain. On real returns the adaptive estimator is more stable under resampling, but, absent a ground truth and in light of the strong-dependence bias, we read that as a variance rather than an accuracy property, and report it as such ( §8).

The open problem that remains is a bandwidth robust across dependence strength. The failure mode is specific: the pointwise-AMSE allocation over-smooths the steep mid-region of a strongly dependent surface, and the oracle-scale experiment of §7.2 shows that no choice of overall scale repairs it; what must change is the shape. That points to an integrated-rather than pointwise-AMISE criterion, or an eff_n-aware bound tied directly to the variance floor of §4. Two further extensions: the exact closed-form constant in the bias functional (5), a full specialization of Hjort and Jones (1996) to the bivariate Gaussian family, would replace the plug-in β with an analytic one; and the same programme extends to the multivariate locally Gaussian density estimator of Otneim and Tjøstheim (2017).
